paragraphs.text: The life of the saints is a rule of living for everyone else. That is why we have received the series of the Scriptures set out so fully: so that, as we come to know Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the other righteous men by reading, we may follow in their shining footsteps the path of innocence that their virtue has, as it were, opened for us. I have often preached on them, and today the story of holy Joseph comes before us. Many kinds of virtue were found in him, but chastity shone out in him above all. So it is right that, having learned from Abraham a tireless devotion of faith, from Isaac the purity of a sincere mind, and from Jacob a singular patience of spirit and in labours, you should now turn your minds from that general account of the virtues to the particular forms of discipline. For although the former are broader, the latter are more sharply drawn, and they penetrate the mind all the more easily the more clearly they are bounded and defined.

Let holy Joseph, then, be set before us as a mirror of chastity. For in his character and in his actions modesty shines out, and alongside chastity there gleams a certain radiance of grace. That is why his parents loved him more than their other sons. But this aroused envy, a point that must not be passed over in silence.

From here, then, the whole plot of the story unfolded, and at the same time we learn that a perfect man is not moved by the wrong done to him to seek revenge for his pain, nor does he repay evil for evil. So David too says: "If I have repaid those who rendered evil to me." For what would have earned Joseph his preference over the others if he had only wounded those who wounded him or loved those who loved him? Most people do that. But it is wonderful if you love your enemy, as the Saviour teaches. So the man who did this before the Gospel is rightly to be admired: wronged, he spared; attacked, he forgave; sold, he did not repay the injury but returned kindness for insult. All of us have learned this since the Gospel, and yet we cannot keep it.

Let us learn, then, about the envy found even among the saints, so that we may imitate their patience, and let us recognize that they were not of a superior nature but of superior diligence, and that they did not know nothing of vices but corrected them. And if envy scorched even the saints, how much more must we take care that it does not set sinners ablaze?

We are taught, then, what the affection of parents ought to be in their favour toward their children. To love one's children is sweet, and to love them more intensely is sweeter still; but often a father's very love, unless it keeps to moderation, harms the children, either when excessive indulgence makes the beloved child slack, or when preferring one turns the others away from brotherly affection. A son gains more when he gains the love of his brothers. This is the more splendid generosity of fathers; this is the richer inheritance of sons. Let equal favour unite the children whom equal nature has united. Devotion knows nothing of a monetary gain that costs a loss of devotion. Why are you surprised if quarrels arise between brothers over a farm or a house, when envy blazed up among the sons of holy Jacob over a tunic?

What then? Is Jacob to be blamed for preferring one son to the rest? But we cannot take from parents the freedom to love more those whom they believe to deserve more, nor should we cut off in children the eagerness to please more. Indeed Jacob loved more the son in whom he foresaw greater marks of virtue, so that it seems less a father preferring a son than a prophet preferring a mystery. And rightly he made him a many-coloured tunic, to signify that, clothed in a variety of virtues, he was to be preferred to his brothers.

Indeed, divine grace shone out in him while he was still a boy. He dreamed that, as it seemed to him in a vision, when he had bound sheaves with his brothers, his sheaf rose up and stood upright, and his brothers' sheaves turned and bowed down to his sheaf. In this the future resurrection of the Lord Jesus was certainly revealed. When the eleven disciples saw him at Jerusalem they worshipped him, and all the saints, when they rise again, will worship him, presenting the fruits of their good works, as it is written: "But coming they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves." So his brothers, although out of envy they denied that the dream could be trusted, nonetheless expressed its interpretation in their own words when they answered him: "Shall you indeed reign over us, or shall you indeed have dominion over us?" For that vision signified the King who was to come, whom all flesh of the human race would worship on bended knee.

Then he saw another dream and told it to his father and his brothers: the sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to him. So his father rebuked him, saying: "What is this vision that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers come and bow down to you on the earth?" Who is it whom parents and brothers worshipped on the earth, if not Christ Jesus, when Joseph and his mother, together with the disciples, worshipped him, confessing the true God in that body? Of him alone it was said: "Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light." And what does the father's rebuke signify, if not the hardness of the people of Israel, from whom Christ came according to the flesh? To this day they do not believe him to be God, nor will they worship him as Lord, because they know that he was born from among them. So they hear his answers and do not understand; they themselves read that the sun and moon praise him, but they refuse to believe that this was said of Christ. Thus Jacob is mistaken in a figure that belongs to another, but he is not mistaken in his own love. His fatherly devotion does not go astray; rather, the attitude of a people that would go astray is being expressed.

So it is not that the patriarch disbelieved so great a dream. He was prophesying both things at once in a twofold oracle, representing both the person of the righteous and that of the people: that the Son of God would come to earth, to be loved by the righteous and denied by the faithless. He saw, then, the mysteries of the future Incarnation when he sent his son to his brothers to see whether the sheep were well. What sheep was God already seeking even then through the patriarch's concern, if not those of whom the Lord Jesus himself said in the Gospel: "I have come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel"? "And he sent him," it says, "to Shechem," which is interpreted "shoulder" or "back": that is, to those who would not turn to the Lord, but fleeing from his face would turn their backs, which is properly the mark of a sinner. For Cain went out from the face of God, and the prophet says: "You will make them turn their back." But the righteous man does not turn away from the Lord; he runs to meet him, saying: "My eyes are ever toward the Lord." And when the Lord said, "Whom shall I send?" Isaiah offered himself of his own accord, saying: "Here am I." And Simeon waited to see Christ the Lord, and after he had seen him, since he had seen the one who forgives sins and the Redeemer of the whole world, he asked, as though relieved of sin, to be released from the use of this flesh, saying: "Now, Lord, let your servant depart, for my eyes have seen your salvation." And Zacchaeus first found the privilege of his commendation in this, that he climbed a tree to see Christ. So Joseph was sent to his brothers by his father, or rather by that Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, that Father of whom it is written: "God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh."

"And Joseph was wandering," it says, because he could not find his brothers. Not without reason did he wander, who was seeking those who had wandered away; for the Lord knows those who are his. So too Jesus, wearied from his journey, sat by the well. He was weary because he did not find the people of God whom he was seeking; for they had gone out from the face of the Lord. Whoever follows guilt goes out from Christ. The sinner goes out; the righteous man goes in. Indeed, Adam the sinner hid himself, but the righteous man says: "Let my plea come into your sight."

Joseph found his brothers in Dothan, which means "failing." For where is the one who deserts God, if not in failing? No wonder those men were failing who did not listen to him who says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." So Joseph came to Dothan, and they saw him coming from far off before he drew near to them, and they raged against him to kill him. Rightly were they far off who were in failing, and they raged because Christ had not drawn near to them. For if the figure of Christ had drawn near to them, they would surely have loved their brother; but those who were plotting fratricide could not be near. "Look," they said, "here comes that dreamer. Come now, let us kill him." Were these not the words of men plotting the sacrilege of fratricide, just as Solomon says of them:

"Let us get rid of the righteous man, for he is useless to us"? And in Genesis they added: "And we shall see what will become of his dreams." This was written of Joseph and fulfilled in Christ, when the Jews said at his Passion: "If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants him." Were those brothers really so wicked as to kill their brother? And then how could such great patriarchs have the merit that the Law should name the tribes of the whole people after them? How can names of piety and the marks of crime fit together? Rather, these men too laboured under the figure of the people, not under a fault of their own minds. From this came all the envy, from this the plotting of fratricide: the envy belonged to the figure, the devotion to their own affection.

Indeed Reuben and Judah, keeping the sacred rights of brotherhood, wished to free him from their hands. And rightly Judah is given precedence in his father's blessing when it is said to him: "Your father's sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion's whelp, and he is the expectation of the nations." This surely fits Christ alone, for whom it was reserved to be worshipped by his brothers and awaited by the nations, and to wash his robe in wine by the suffering of his own body, since he stained his flesh with no blemish of sin. Nor did Asher believe that these words applied to himself: "Asher, his bread is rich, and he himself, Asher, with princes [?]." And what of Joseph himself, to whom it was said: "My son who is to be increased, Joseph, my son who is to be increased, my envied son, my youngest son, return to me; against whom they took counsel and reviled him; in whom the blessing prevailed over the blessings of the abiding mountains and the desires of the everlasting hills"? Whom did he understand to be signified in himself, if not the one who, surpassing the merits of all, above the desires of all the saints, would hold the summit of boundless power, whom no one could equal even in wish? So the envy of the patriarchs is outweighed by grace: they are both excused from guilt and consecrated by the gift of revelation. For it is not so blameworthy to have spoken the words that belong to the people as it is blessed to have seen the things that belong to Christ. They took on the role of a sinful people in order to receive the grace of the Lord the Redeemer. Certainly grace has blotted out the guilt, and the guilt has not lessened the grace.

And so that we may recognize that all this is a mystery concerning the people and the Lord Jesus, he says: "Come, let us sell Joseph to the Ishmaelites." What does the name Joseph mean in interpretation, if not that it signifies divine grace and the image of the most high God? Who, then, is sold, if not he who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? For we would not have bought him if his own had not sold him. They sold badly; they bought worse. They sold to merchants; the merchants bought a good fragrance from traitors. For Judah sold, and the Ishmaelites bought, who in Latin interpretation signify "those who hate their God." That is why we find Joseph bought in one place for twenty gold pieces, in another for twenty-five, in another for thirty: because Christ is not worth one and the same price to everyone. To some he is worth less, to others more. The buyer's faith increases the value of the goods. God is more precious to the more devout; the Redeemer is more precious to the sinner. He is worth more to the one who has more grace; but he is also worth more to the one to whom much has been forgiven, because the one to whom more is forgiven loves more. So the Lord himself declared in the Gospel about the woman who poured ointment on his feet, washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and dried them with her kisses, of whom he said to Simon: "Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom less is forgiven loves less." Sometimes, too, the differences in price express not only an amount but also a number, as you find with the ointment which the Lord said had been poured out for his burial, when Judas, as it is written, said: "This could have been sold for three hundred denarii." In that number what seems to be expressed is not an amount but a sign of the cross. So here too the difference between twenty and thirty gold or silver pieces indicates a double or a threefold perfection. And the twenty-five gold pieces of the jubilee, which is the number of remission, signify a most precious portion. Here too, so that you may notice the figure of the Lord's Passion, the patriarch Judah says: "Let us hand Joseph over to the Ishmaelites, but let our hands not be laid upon him." And earlier it had well been said, "Do not lay your hands on him"—just as the Jews said at the Lord's Passion: "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death," so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, signifying by what death he was to die.

Even then, therefore, the sign of the future cross was being prefigured, and at the same time the fact that he was stripped of his tunic—that is, of the flesh he had taken on—stripped of the beautiful variety of virtues. So it was his tunic, that is, his flesh, not his divinity, that was stained with blood; they could take from him the garment of flesh, but not the immortality of life. This tunic was bloodied by the Jewish beasts, those of whom he says:

"Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves." And as for the pit being dry, what wonder if the pit of the Jews has no water, since they have forsaken the fountain of living water and made for themselves broken cisterns? And so that you may know this is truly a mystery, the Lord himself says of himself: "They have laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death."

Those, then, buy Christ who bring good fragrances: incense, with which they make offerings on the altars of a devout mind—which is why David says in Greek: "Let my prayer be directed like incense before you"—and also resin, with which broken pieces of marble are joined together. There is a spiritual resin that can make firm the fractures of your soul, join what has been torn apart, and bind together what has come loose. This spiritual resin strengthens and sets the shattered limbs of the soul, so that they are joined without hurt. Indeed, Jeremiah seeks it in his effort to heal Babylon, if he can, saying: "Take resin for her corruption, if perhaps she may be healed. We treated Babylon, and she was not healed." The synagogue was not healed, because this resin had passed over to the Church. That is why the merchants came from Gilead—that is, from the possession or dwelling-place of testimony—carrying their wares over to the Church, so that this resin might heal the sins of the nations, to whom it is said: "Grow strong, you weak hands and feeble knees." Sincere faith is this resin. Peter applied it when he said to the lame man: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk." And rightly he rose and walked. He had it when he said to the paralytic: "Aeneas, the Lord Jesus heals you; rise and make your bed." And he rose and made his bed. He had it when he said to the dead woman: "Rise in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ." And the dead woman rose. By the blending of this resin those stones are bonded together from which God is able to raise up children to Abraham. By the healing power of this resin the lame man is set upright, the paralytic restored, the dead woman raised to life.

The fact that they spattered his tunic with a goat's blood also seems to signify that, attacking him with false witnesses, they brought the odium of sin upon the one who forgives the sins of all. To us he is a lamb, to them a goat. For us the Lamb of God was slain, for us whose sins of the world he took away; for them he is a goat, for he heaped up their errors and piled up their offences. That is why he says: "Fill up the measure of your fathers." And rightly Jacob, lamenting the loss of his posterity, wept as a father for a lost son and mourned as a prophet for the destruction of the Jews. Indeed, he even tore his garment—which we read was done at the Passion of the Lord Jesus by the high priest, who acted there not as a private person but in the duty of public office. And the veil of the Temple was torn, so that by such signs it might be made plain that the mysteries had been profaned, the people stripped of their saving garments, and the kingdom divided and doomed to destruction, because every kingdom divided against itself is easily destroyed. And it was truly divided when what had been Christ's began to be the devil's. For those who were separating the Son from the Father could not remain undivided.

So Joseph was sold, taken to Egypt, and bought by the chief of the cooks. This is no idle figure: a cook who would cook what was raw, so that minds might feast on the sweetness of faith; for no food is sweeter than knowledge and teaching. Before this there was in Egypt a raw faithlessness, which no ardour for the knowledge of God and no desire for true understanding had softened, and which the fiery words of the Lord had not cooked through. Joseph was sold into Egypt because Christ was to come to those to whom it was said: "You were sold for your sins." And so with his own blood he redeemed those whom their own sins had sold. But Christ was sold by taking on our condition, not by guilt; he is not held by the price of sin, because he himself committed no sin. So by that price he took on our debt, not debts of his own: he removed the bond, sent away the moneylender, and set the debtor free. One man paid off what was owed by all. We were not allowed to go out of slavery; he took this upon himself for us, to drive away the slavery of the world, to restore the freedom of paradise, and to bestow a new grace with the honour of fellowship with himself. So much for the mystery.

As for the moral sense, since the Lord our God wills all to be saved, through Joseph he also gave comfort to those in slavery and provided them with instruction, so that they might learn that even in the lowest condition one's character can be superior, and that no state is closed off from virtue if each person's mind knows itself: that the flesh is subject to slavery, not the mind; and that many slaves are freer than their masters if, though placed in slavery, they hold that they must refrain from slavish deeds. Every sin is slavish; innocence is free. So the Lord too says: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin." For how is every greedy man not a slave, who auctions himself off for a little profit of money? He who has heaped up what he will not use fears everything, lest he lose what he has heaped up; and the more he has acquired, the greater the danger in which he keeps it. How is he not a beggar to whom what he possesses seems little? For even if he seems rich to me, to himself he is in want, and he cannot console his longings with any proof, since he cannot believe he has what he desires. And how is the man who is subject to lust not a slave too? First, he burns in his own fires and is scorched by the torches of his own heart. To such the prophet rightly says: "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled." He takes on every fear; he lies in wait for the sleep of each person in order to win the object of his desire for one; he becomes the slave of all. He serves, then, and in a wretched slavery, who makes masters for himself and chooses to have people to fear; for nothing is so characteristic of slavery as always being afraid. But he is always free, in whatever condition of slavery, who is not captured by love, not held by the chains of greed, not bound by fear of guilt, who looks on the present without anxiety and is not terrified by the future. Does it not seem to you that the one rules while in slavery, and the other is a slave while in freedom? Joseph was a slave, Pharaoh was a king: happier was the one's slavery than the other's kingship. Indeed, all Egypt would have collapsed from famine had Pharaoh not submitted his kingdom to the counsel of a slave.

So slaves by birth have something to boast of: Joseph too was a slave. Those who have passed from freedom into slavery through some misfortune have something to console themselves with. They have someone to imitate, so that they may learn that their condition can change but not their character, and that there is freedom even among household slaves and steadfastness even in slavery. Masters, too, have reason to hope for good things through good slaves. Abraham found a wife for his son through a household slave. The Lord blessed the Egyptian's house because of Joseph, and the Lord's blessing was on all his property, both in the house and in the fields. "And he turned over," it says, "everything he had into Joseph's hands." We observe that what the masters could not manage, the slaves managed.

But why should I point to how this young slave managed a private household, when he went on to rule an empire? Yet it is a greater thing that he first ruled himself. He was handsome to look at and very fair of face, but he did not turn the beauty of his face to another's harm. He kept it for his own grace, thinking himself the more beautiful if he proved fairer not by losing his chastity but by cultivating modesty. True beauty, he held, is the kind that does not capture other people's eyes or wound weak minds, but wins the good judgment of all, a snare to no one and a credit to oneself. If some woman looked at him with wanton eyes, the guilt belongs only to her who looked wrongly, not to him who did not wish to be looked at wrongly; there is no fault in having been seen. It was not in the young slave's power to avoid being seen: the husband ought to have watched his wife's eyes. If the husband feared nothing from his wife, Joseph took this as a testimony to his own chastity, not as a license for carelessness. Still, let men too learn to beware of women's eyes; even those who do not wish to be loved are loved passionately. Joseph was in fact passionately loved, though he scorned the woman who loved him. And Scripture rightly excused him when it said: "His master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph." That is, he did not show himself off or capture her unawares. She cast her own nets and was caught in her own toils; she spread her snares and was entangled in her own bonds.

"And she said to him: Lie with me." The first weapons of the adulteress are those of the eyes, the second [?]; but one who is not captured by the eyes can resist a word. Defense is still at hand while the affections are still free. That is why it is written that he refused. First, then, he overcame her in the contest of the mind, driving back her attack as with the shield of his spirit. Then he hurled his speech like a spear, to make her draw back. "And he said to his master's wife." She is rightly called his master's wife and not herself his mistress, since she could not wring from him what she wanted to obtain. How could she be a mistress, when she had no power to command, when she did not keep the discipline proper to a mistress, when she offered her slaves the incitements of lust? He was the master, who did not catch the flames of her love, who did not feel the bonds of her enticement, whom no fear of death could terrify, who preferred to die free of crime rather than choose partnership with a guilty power. He was free, for he held it shameful not to return favor for favor. And so he does not make excuses like a timid man, nor is he on his guard like one afraid of danger; rather, as one indebted to his master's kindness and to his own innocence, he flees the crime of ingratitude, and as a just man he shudders at the stain of sin and the contagion of guilt. The adulteress hurled a third dart by pestering him persistently. "But Joseph would not listen to her." Here you learn what to beware of after the first words. Lust is not only slippery but also bold, importunate and wanton, and an adulteress has nothing to feel ashamed of. A woman who did not grieve over the first loss of her modesty lies in wait to make her catch.

Then, when he had gone in to attend to his duty and the task entrusted to him, she seized him, with witnesses and servants out of the way, and said: "Lie with me." Joseph is excused by the testimony of Scripture, since he could not neglect the service his master had entrusted to him. It is not enough to say that he entered the inner rooms of the house secure in himself, as one who could not be caught: a just man ought to have taken care not to give her in her frenzy an opportunity, lest she perish through her sin over him. But a man who saw his master's wife set against him also had to guard against offending his master by neglecting his duty. Besides, he still thought her boldness was only a matter of words, not of laying hands on him.

He is excused for going in; he is praised for escaping, and for valuing the garments of the body less than the chastity of the soul. He left behind, as if they were not his own, the clothes the adulteress was holding in her hands, and judged that whatever could be grasped by the touch of a shameless woman belonged to someone else. A great man indeed: sold as a slave, he knew nothing of a slave's character; passionately loved, he did not love in return; entreated, he did not consent; seized, he fled. When his master's wife accosted him, she could hold him by his garment but could not capture him in his mind. He did not even put up with her words for long, judging it a contagion to stay any longer, lest the incitements of lust pass to him through the hands of the adulteress. So he took off his garment and shook off the crime. Leaving behind the cloak by which he was held, he fled stripped indeed, but not naked, for he was better covered by the garment of modesty. No one is naked except the one whom guilt has stripped. Earlier in Scripture we read that Adam, after he abandoned God's commandments by transgression and contracted the debt of grievous sin, was naked. So he himself says: "I heard your voice in paradise and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid myself." He realized that he was naked because he had lost the insignia of divine protection. And he hid because he did not have the garment of faith, which he had cast off by his transgression. See what a great thing this is. The one who was naked had not lost his tunic; the one who was not naked had taken off his clothes and left them in the hands of the adulteress. The same Scripture declared the first naked and denied that the second was. So Joseph stripped himself rather than made himself naked, for he kept the garments of the virtues uncorrupted, stripping off the old man with his deeds so as to put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator. Adam, however, remained naked, for he could not clothe himself again once he had been stripped of the singular robe of virtue. That is why he received a tunic of skins: as a sinner he could not have a spiritual one. So Joseph left his garments behind and laid bare the shamelessness of the adulteress, which afterwards could not stay hidden.

Then she went outside and, raising her voice, made public her own attempt at adultery, saying that the Hebrew had left his clothes and fled. So she herself betrayed what she ought to have concealed, in order to harm an innocent man with a trumped-up charge. But a just man does not know how to accuse, and so the shameless woman did this with impunity. I would say that she was the one truly stripped, though she held someone else's clothes, for she had lost every covering of chastity; and that he was well enough adorned and well enough defended, for his voice was not heard but his innocence spoke. So later Susanna, keeping silent at her trial, spoke more eloquently through a divine oracle, and because she did not seek the help of her own voice, she earned a prophet as her defender. I would say, then, that Joseph was the more blessed when he was sent to prison, because he was undergoing martyrdom for chastity. Chastity is a good gift, but of lesser merit when it faces no danger; when it is defended even at the risk of one's life, then it is more fully crowned. Without a hearing, without inquiry into the truth, Joseph is sent to prison as if guilty of the crime; but the Lord did not desert him even in prison. Let the innocent not be dismayed when they are assailed with false charges, when justice is crushed and they are thrust into prison.

God visits his own even in prison, and so there is more help where there is more danger. But what wonder is it if Christ visits those in prison, when he declared that he himself was shut in prison in the persons of his own, as you have it written: "I was in prison, and you did not come to me"? Where does divine mercy not penetrate? Joseph found such favor that he who had been shut in prison came instead to keep the prison's locks: the jailer gave up his office and put all the prisoners in Joseph's charge. So not only did Joseph not feel the prison, but he even relieved others of the prison's hardships.

The authors of this injustice, then, are a woman and eunuchs. But the woman is one of those Egyptian women who are given to bold talk with men, to provoking the modest, pursuing those who flee and pressing hard on those who feel shame. Since she could not defend her own vices, she accused the innocent, adding treachery to treachery, holding what belonged to another, condemning others herself, and setting no limit to her fury. For what reason was there for her cruelty, except that she saw her desires opposed and her longings cheated by a refusal of consent? See why the prison is opened: to receive the innocent. Chains are loosed from the guilty to be put on the faithful; adulterers of the truth are set free so that he who refused to adulterate his faithfulness may be locked up.

And what shall I say of those eunuchs? They ought to serve as an example to other eunuchs, for their position is fragile and slight, all their hope lies in the will of the king, a slight offense means the gravest danger for them, and their prosperity is but a lowly service. One boasted that he was in charge of the wine, the other that he was in charge of the bakers. Both gave offense and were sent to prison, and were put in the charge of holy Joseph by the keeper of the prison himself. When they had been there a good many days, they had a dream. And when Joseph came to see them again, he found them sad and troubled in mind, because they were disturbed by a dream for which they could find no interpreter. "Does not the interpretation of a dream come through God?" he said. "Tell it to me, then." And the chief of the wine told his dream: "There was a vine before me, and on the vine three roots, and it was blossoming and putting forth shoots, and the clusters of grapes were ripe, and Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. And I took the grapes and pressed them into the cup and gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand." And Joseph said to him: "The three roots are three days. Within three more days Pharaoh will remember your office and restore you to your former post, and you will give the cup into Pharaoh's hand. But remember me yourself when it goes well with you, and show me mercy, and remember me to Pharaoh and bring me out of this prison, for I was stolen away by theft from the land of the Hebrews, and here I have done nothing wrong, but they have put me into this prison pit."

I have no wish to speak of the other man's dream. You certainly remember my words: even then I shrank from interpreting it with reference to that man whose end I shrink from, whose death I shudder at. Let us speak first of the one who thought himself fortunate because he was in charge of the wine, and believed it the very summit of all power that he handed the king his cup. This was his glory, this his grandeur in this world: deprived of it he grieved, restored to it he rejoiced. But this is a dream, and all the power of this world is a dream, not reality. Indeed, it was in a dream that he saw his office restored to him. And Isaiah says that men who delight in prosperity in this world are like this. Just as someone who eats and drinks in his sleep seems, while he sleeps, to be filled with food or drink, but when he wakes begins to be hungrier still, and then realizes how empty was the food and drink of his dream, so whoever sleeps in this world and does not open his eyes to the divine mysteries thinks, as long as he is weighed down by the sleep of the body, that this worldly power is of some importance, since he sees it as in a dream; but when he wakes, he discovers how empty the pleasure of this world is.

Consider now that true Hebrew, the interpreter not of a dream but of the truth and of a glorious vision, who came from that fullness of divinity and freedom of heavenly grace into this prison of the body. The allurements of this world could not change him, nor could any corruption of worldly pleasure overthrow him. Tempted, he did not fall; desired, he did not desire. At last, seized by the garment of his body by the adulterous hand, as it were, of the synagogue, he put off the flesh and rose free of death. The harlot slandered him when she could not hold him, him whom prison did not terrify. The underworld did not hold him; indeed, from the place to which he had gone down as if for punishment, he set others free.

Where the bonds of death were being tightened on him, there he loosed the bonds of the dead. Consider, then, this Hebrew saying to the chief of the eunuchs, who had incurred the king's displeasure and whom he had restored to his office: "Remember me yourself when it goes well with you, and show me mercy, and remember me." He said it a second time because he knew that once the man had recovered his power he would not remember what disgrace he had escaped. He warned him a second time because he had freed him a second time, so that if the memory of the first kindness did not hold him, that of the second might come to mind, and he would not despise the author of his deliverance or wrong him by faithless betrayal. But what is worse, forgetfulness of a kindness quickly creeps in with prosperity. Restored to his office, he did not remember the interpreter but forgot him. Yet even if he forgot, Christ did not forget; he spoke to him, and spoke through the young slave, saying to him: "Remember me yourself," that is: at least out of regard for your office, recall what you heard. "But even if you have forgotten now, you will remember me," so that you who forgot the kindness may escape the danger. Yet, puffed up by his power, he did not remember. And how great is this power, which consists in serving wine? See where all the boasting comes from! He was chief of the eunuchs who served wine in the royal cups.

"And it came to pass," it says, "after two years." Call me a liar about this, about the time of our own eunuch, if even the date does not agree: for after two years he recovered his office, and he did not remember until he was reminded. He who did not believe his own dream came to know that even kingship itself is a dream in this world. He also learned that the [?] of kings are dreams and that their powers are not everlasting. But let grief pass quickly over this matter, so that it is not made raw again by recalling it. It gives me no pleasure even to remember my own words, which at that time grief poured out of me, or the insult to the Church wrung from me.

So, reminded of Joseph by the king's dream, he says: "I remember my sin." A late confession, but would that it were a true one! After the sin you confess what you should have guarded against before the sin. How quickly you forgot "Remember me"! You know, of course, that these were the words spoken at that time, but your ears were dulled by the pride of power, and drunk with wine you did not hear the words of sobriety. Remember me now at least, you who confess your sin so late. You who make requests of the young slave, why do you deny his Lord? Be drunk now, not with wine, but with the Holy Spirit. Remember what happened to the man with whom you slept your sleep and dreamed your dream. He too was a chief, chief of the king's fare that belonged to the bakers' work. He thought himself exalted because he had the king's bread in his power: he did not know how many twists and turns this power has. He threatened others, though he himself was soon to be handed over to the ultimate penalty, and he did not listen to the one who, though a young slave, nevertheless spoke the Lord's oracle: that by the order of the very king in whom he took such pride he would lose his head and be left as food for the birds. This example at least should have called you back, so that you would not put your trust in faithlessness.

There are other examples too of the pride and fragility of royal ministers, which the history of a later period contains. Doeg too was a chief, chief over the king's beasts, for the training of mules, that is, of eunuch animals. He also informed against a priest of the Lord and by his deceit stirred up the king to endanger the priest, and he too was a Syrian. Am I lying, when both his country and his deeds agree? Haman too, the king's chamberlain and himself a chief, when with shameless rashness he strove to attack the churches of the Lord and to plunder and persecute the faithful people, paid for his sacrileges with severe punishment.

But let us return to this chief of the wine, who, as though drunk with much wine, long forgot the author of his kindness. At last, however, to provide the king with an interpreter, he related the course of events, not out of gratitude but out of shrewdness. Learning of this, the king too ordered Joseph to be summoned, and when he had been brought out of prison asked him whether he could interpret his dream for him. Delighted with his explanation, he removed his disgrace and conferred honor on him. See, then, whether these things also do not fit present events. The injury was done before the king came to know him; favor was returned once the king knew him. So the king is free from blame, because the injury the holy man suffered came from others, and the favor he received is the king's own.

Now the dream and its interpretation are as follows: "Whatever God does," he said, "he has shown to Pharaoh. The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years. Pharaoh's dream is one. And the seven lean cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven ears that were thin and blighted by the wind are seven years. There will be seven years of famine. As for the word I spoke, 'Whatever God does he has shown to Pharaoh': behold, seven years of great plenty are coming throughout the whole land of Egypt; but after these will come seven years of famine, and they will forget the plenty in all Egypt. And the famine will consume the whole land, and the plenty in the land will not be recognized because of the famine that will follow, for it will be very severe. And the dream was repeated to Pharaoh twice because the word from God will be true, and God will hasten to do it."

An old dream, but recent events. What came first was consumed by what came after, and where there had been abundant plenty, there came want of everything. If someone had given the ruler advice of this kind, to keep something from the earlier plenty for the later period of his reign, then the remaining time too would have overflowed with a lavish abundance for giving. But the immoderate squandering of the earlier age left the later one destitute too, and men who were plundering everything would not call in any Joseph. Although I am no Joseph (for who could claim that?), I nevertheless cried out that those fat cows signified not only wantonness but also neglect of reverence for God (for of the faithless it is said: "Fat bulls have besieged me," and of the Jewish people it is written: "He grew fat and stout and broad, and forsook God who made him"), and that therefore that dream of worldly abundance could not last forever: a time would come when harsh famine would follow for them.

Yet I do not think that this dream was shown to one or two only, but set before all, in that the seven years of this world, fat and rich with worldly plenty, are to be swallowed up by the ages to come, in which there is everlasting rest and the spiritual observance of the law. That observance is kept by Ephraim, that tribe of the patriarchs fruitful to God, the good cow, not swollen with a bodily udder but abounding in spiritual milk and grace, on the beauty of whose neck God says he sits, as it is written: "Ephraim is a heifer trained to love victory, and I passed over the beauty of her neck." So let not the oil of the sinner anoint our head, and let false fruits not delight us, lest it be said of us too: "You have sown ungodliness and harvested its iniquities; you have eaten false fruit, because you hoped in your chariots." Nor does it trouble me that the dream has thin ears blighted by the wind, for David too was better when he was wasting away like a spider, and "a troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God," and those whom the evil spirit has tried with grievous injuries in this world come out the stronger.

That is why I think Joseph earned mystical rewards, because he spoke of mystical things. For what does the ring put on his finger mean, if not that we should understand that the high priesthood of faith was conferred on him, so that he might seal others? What does the robe mean, which is the clothing of wisdom, if not that the heavenly King granted him preeminence in understanding? The golden necklace seems to express good understanding, and the chariot signifies the lofty height of his merits. And who is it that took a wife from the Gentiles, if not he who gathered to himself a Church from the nations, and received from her a son, Manasseh, through whom he forgot all the sorrows he had suffered from the sacrileges of the Jews? He also received another son, Ephraim, through whose growth it became clear that the humility assumed in the flesh did not humble his divinity but heaped up his glory.

Then all who were suffering famine were sent to Joseph. Who are these if not those of whom it was said: "They will return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs"? Now the famine was not in one place but over the whole earth, for there was no one who did good. Therefore the Lord [?]Jesus, taking pity on the world's hunger, opened his storehouses and laid open the hidden treasures of the heavenly mysteries, of knowledge and wisdom, so that no one should lack food. For Wisdom said: "Come, eat my bread," and so only the one who is filled by Christ can say: "The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing." Christ, then, opened his storehouses and sold, seeking not money but the price of faith and the payment of devotion. And he sold not to a few in Judea but to all, so that he might be believed in by all the nations.

And all the lands came into Egypt to Joseph to buy, for the famine had prevailed. For all whom Christ has not fed go hungry. Let us buy food, then, with which we can drive away hunger. Let no one be held back by thinking of his poverty; let no one who has no silver be afraid. Christ does not ask for silver but for faith, which is more precious than silver. Peter, indeed, bought him, though he had no silver: "Silver and gold I do not have," he said, "but what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk." And the prophet Isaiah says: "You who thirst, go to the water, and all you who have no silver, go, buy, and drink and eat, without silver and without the price of wine." For he who paid the price of his own blood for us did not ask a price from us, since he redeemed us not with gold and silver but with precious blood. So you owe the price with which you were bought. Even if he does not always demand it, you still owe it. Buy Christ for yourself, then, not with what few have, but with what all have by nature, though few offer it, out of fear. What Christ asks back from you is his own. He gave life to all; he offered his death for all. Pay for your Author what you will in any case pay by law. This is no ordinary bargain, and not everyone sees it easily. Indeed, those virgins in the Gospel whom the bridegroom shut out on his coming were left outside because they had not bought the oil that was for sale. And so it is said to them: "Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves." And the merchant who sold all he had and bought the pearl is praised, and rightly so.

And Jacob said to his sons: "Why are you idle? See, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy food for us." Jacob did not say this only once; every day he says to all his sons who are slow to come to the grace of Christ: "Why are you idle? See, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt." From this grain comes the seed that rises again.

So whoever suffers hunger must lay it to his own sloth. "See," he says, "I have heard that there is grain in Egypt." Young men usually hear things sooner than old men, since many of them are out and about. But it is the old man who first hears of this trade—yet that old man in whom the grey hair of faith is long-lived; it is the old man who first understands, the old man in whom old age is venerable, and "a spotless life is ripe old age." Nor does anyone take up this trade except the sons of Jacob, and they of more advanced age. That is why ten go, and the youngest does not go. His father did not send him: "lest some harm befall him," he said. Benjamin, the youngest, was still liable to weakness. Benjamin is read of as a patriarch, but in him Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, was prefigured. Jacob had good reason to be anxious about his weakness. And in fact he was made weak so that he might be healed: he suffered blindness, but this weakness led to salvation; that blindness, indeed, brought light. We have taken in the story; let us come to know the mystery.

The patriarchs had first set out without Benjamin, the apostles without Paul. Neither arrived first, but each, summoned by those who came first, made the goods of the earlier ones more abundant by his coming. "There is grain in Egypt," he says; that is, where the famine is greater, there the abundance is greater. There is great grain in Egypt. Indeed, God the Father too says: "Out of Egypt I called my son." From that grain comes that fruitfulness, for there could have been no harvest unless the Egyptians had first sown the seed. So there is grain which no one before believed existed; in this grain the patriarchs trade. They had indeed brought silver, but the good Joseph gave grain and gave back the silver; for Christ is bought not with money but with grace. Your price is faith: with this the divine mysteries are bought. And this grain is carried by that ass which was once unclean under the law but is now clean under grace.

Yet Benjamin, the youngest, was held back and still clung to his father's affection. The bonds of the law held him, the custom of his fathers. The famine grew worse because he was slow in coming. Two plead for him, Reuben and Judah, that is, humility and confession. These he uses as sureties before his father; to these he is entrusted, one of whom is the firstborn and the other the one raised up again: the law belongs to the firstborn, the Gospel to the one raised up. By these Benjamin, the youngest, is brought down, and he arrives accompanied by sweet fragrances, carrying with him resin, by which marble stones are joined together, because he too, by his own preaching, would join living stones together as with a spiritual resin; carrying also honey, by which the poison of a wound is eaten away from within without any harshness of cutting. For such was Paul's preaching that, with the sting of his argument, he did away with diseased affection and drained off the corrupt humor, choosing to cauterize the sick inner parts of the mind rather than to cut them. That the incense of prayer, cassia and stacte are tokens of burial the prophet David taught us, saying: "Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments." For Paul came to preach the cross of the Lord, the evergreen holm oak, and nuts, whose shell is harder and whose fruit is softer—and rightly the priestly rod of Aaron was of nut-wood, and so was the staff of Jeremiah—and double silver too. Who could doubt that these gifts are not without meaning, since both the life of the patriarch and the word of the apostle are ever green in the hearts of each person, and the speech of the saints, like silver tried in the fire, shines with the brightness of saving precept? And it is fitting that those in whom Paul's coming was prefigured bring back double silver, for he granted double honor to presbyters who labor in word and teaching.

And Joseph saw them, and Benjamin his brother, born of the same mother. Now the Hebrews are seen, and seen by Christ, who is the true Joseph, when they come in the figure of Paul; and he speaks gentle and kindly words to them, so that they may take food together. Earlier, however, because they had come without Benjamin, he did recognize them but turned away from them, as it is written: "and he spoke harshly to them," because they did not recognize the one by whom they were recognized. So they made progress through the merit of Paul, whom the Lord Jesus loved more than the other brothers, as a younger brother born of the same mother. Let the Jews take note of the Lord whom they denied. Even though crucified by their synagogue, he still loves them all the more as sprung from the same parent, if only they would recognize, however late, the author of their salvation. But conscious of their own offenses, they do not believe that Christ's mercy is so great that he forgives sin and pardons injury. And so what they would be like was prefigured in the patriarchs. They were invited to grace, called to the feast of the saving table, and they suspected that a false charge was being prepared against them and a trap laid.

And they began to want to plead their case with the man who was over the house, at the door of the house. They still hesitate to go in; those who wish to argue their case would rather be justified by their own works than receive grace, and so they are refuted at the gates. But he who awaits the fruit of the virgin womb and the inheritance of the Lord, who trades for the reward of the Son, is not put to shame at the gate, but at the departure from this life drives back the enemy, so that the enemy, aware of some graver fault, may not stand in his way as he hastens to higher things.

Hence, in a mystical sense, the steward of the house answered them. Understand who he is when you read of Moses, faithful in all his house. For Moses, Peter, Paul and the other saints are stewards of the house, but Christ alone is the Lord. It is written that Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, to bear witness to the things that were to be spoken, but Christ as a son over his own house; and we are that house, if we hold fast the freedom and the glory of hope.

This steward of the house, then, answered them: "May God be gracious to you; do not be afraid. For your God and the God of your fathers gave you treasures in your sacks; I have received your silver, and it was good." For they had said: "We found each man's silver in our sacks. We have brought back our silver in full weight." O great mysteries, and plainly expressed! It is as if to say: Why are you puffed up? Why do you so often claim that you have your own silver in your sacks? "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? Already you are filled; already you have become rich." You who believe you have silver—it was the God of your fathers who gave you the silver. He is your God, he is the God of your fathers, whom you denied. But he forgives, he pardons, he takes you back, if you return. He it is who does not seek your silver but gives his own. He himself gave you the silver in your sacks. Now your sacks, which held mud, hold silver; and so he is yours who says: "You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness." Christ is the gift of gladness. He is your silver, he is your price. The Lord Jesus does not demand from you the price of his grain; he does not seek the weight of your silver.

Your silver is rejected; the silver of the sack is not good. "I have received your silver, and it was good"—that is, not that material silver, but your spiritual silver, which is good, which you brought with faithful devotion as sons of Jacob, which is given without loss and counted out without any cost, since by such a price the damage of death is shut out and the gain of life is acquired.
And they made ready the gifts until Joseph came in at noon.

Paul's faith hastened the noon. Before, he was blind; afterwards he began to see the light of righteousness, since whoever reveals his way to the Lord and hopes in him, the Lord will bring forth his righteousness like the light and his judgment like the noonday. And when God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, it was noon, and the eternal light shone upon him from the presence of the Lord. It is noon when the true Joseph enters his house to dine. For the day shines more brightly then, when we celebrate the sacraments.

"And they brought him," it says, "the gifts." We bring gifts; he lays out a banquet. He says: "Set out the bread," which only the Hebrews eat, while the Egyptians cannot eat it. But before the banquet, what condescension! What a moral lesson in the practice of such attentiveness and graciousness! The brothers were still suspicious of the false charge they thought Joseph was bringing against them. He invited them to dinner: their feelings wavered, but his graciousness held firm. He is the first to address them, the first to ask: "How are you?"

And again he said: "Is your father, the old man, well?" It belongs to the superior to draw the inferior into conversation, to give him confidence to speak, to ask not only about them but also about their parents.

They answer: "Your servant our father is well." He called him "the old man" to honour him; they called him "servant" to pay the respect of humility, since old age carries a dignity that is honoured, while servanthood is seen as subordinate and closer to modesty than to pride.

And looking up with his eyes he saw Benjamin, his brother by the same mother. It is a moral lesson that we see those we love before all others, and those whom the mind is intent upon are the first to meet our gaze; for often, when the mind is distracted and busy with other things, we do not see those who are right before our eyes. So our sight is directed by the mind as its guide. Holy Joseph therefore saw his brother Benjamin, whom he held in his mind, whom he sought with his eyes, and in whose absence he had scarcely seen his brothers, because seeing them did him no good. And not content merely to have seen him, he asked as though he did not know: "Is this your younger brother?" It is the custom and the grace of love to hold those dear to us not only with our eyes but also with our words. Joseph had recognized his beloved, but he asked so that his voice might utter the one whom his heart held.

Then he did not wait for an answer, but at once blessed him and was troubled by the fulfilment of his longing. His inmost being was in torment, because the freedom to embrace the one he had longed for was being put off. Then he went into an inner room and wept, and washed his face and restrained himself. The stings of great love quickly pierce the heart unless the reins of longing are loosened. Joseph was overcome by his feeling, but held back by his plan: reason contended with love. He wept, to temper the heat of his devoted love with tears.

So much for the moral sense. In the mystical sense, the Lord Jesus saw Paul—for the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous—and said: "Is this your younger brother?" He is still called "younger" because he did not yet bear the mature age of grey-haired faith, had not yet grown into the perfect man, into that measure, as he himself says, of the age of the fullness of Christ. Indeed, he is described as a young man only where he kept the garments of those who were stoning Stephen. And so he wished Philemon to resemble not his youth but his old age, as he wrote: "I rather appeal to you, since you are such a one as Paul, an old man." That is why he teaches that the younger widows are to be avoided, not because of their age, but because of a certain wantonness of youthful sins and immaturity of virtue. Otherwise, the praise of chastity is greater in a young man than in an old one. But I think it is not far from the truth if we understand it this way: when Paul heard [?] this and shuddered under the rebuke, because blindness had befallen him, he nevertheless began to draw near, saying: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" That is why he was called "younger" by Christ: so that one who was being called to grace might be excused from guilt, because it had belonged to a slippery age. Then Christ saw him, when the light shone around him; and because young men are recalled from vice more by fear than by reason, he applied the goad and in his mercy warned him not to kick against the goad.

And he was troubled, just as you have in the gospel that he troubled himself in spirit when he raised Lazarus, and there he wept, so that he might first wash away the dead man's sins with his tears. But he wept inside, and washed his face. Paul's blindness is Christ's weeping: he washes his face when the lost light is restored to him. Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus would be seen by many. And so at the banquet his portion was made five times greater, because he would be preferred above those who came before him not only for wisdom of mind but also for the discipline of his body and the grace of chastity.

And they drank and were made drunk together with him. From the beginning of his faith a greater privilege is conferred on Paul, of whom it was said to Ananias: "Go, for he is a chosen vessel to me, to bear my name before the Gentiles." From the beginning he is made drunk with a drunkenness, but a sober one, so that he too might say with the saints: "And your cup that inebriates, how glorious it is!"

And the silver cup is put into his sack alone. Benjamin did not know this: Paul was being deceived, but he was being called. They are sent after him in the morning; for the night of blindness was far spent, and the day of faith was drawing near.

The sacks of each are first searched in order. Divine Scripture teaches you a moral lesson. Earlier they had reclined at the banquet in order facing him, the firstborn according to his age. You see that the first place is to be given to the elder. Again the sacks of each are searched in order, so that you may know that Paul was chosen by heavenly judgment. He examined the others; he preferred this one. In no one else's sack was the silver cup found but in his. What does it mean that it was put into his sack? Joseph indeed made them drunk in order to deceive them, and sent the cup so that by a loving trick he might call back the brother he loved; but the divine mysteries shine through.

Christ finds in us this silver, which he himself has given. We have the silver of nature, and we have the silver of grace. Nature is the work of the Creator; grace is the gift of the Redeemer. Even if we cannot see the gifts of Christ, he nevertheless gives them and works in secret, and he gives to all, but it belongs to few to keep them and not lose them. Yet he does not give everything to everyone. Wheat is given to many, the cup to one, who is endowed with the prophetic and priestly gift. For not everyone, but the prophet says: "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord."

So in Paul's body the utterance of heavenly teaching was already shining, since he was learned in the law. But because he was not yet subject to the righteousness of God, the cup was inside the sack, the teaching inside the law, the lamp under the bushel. Yet Ananias was sent to give the blessing, to lay on his hand, to untie the sack. When the sack was untied the silver shone out, and as the scales fell away, like the cords of a sack, at once he saw. His bond was unbelief; his release came about through faith. And so, as though the sack had been untied—that is, the veil of the law that lies over the heart of the Jews having been laid aside—turned to the Lord, free of the bond and having obtained the grace of freedom, he says: "And so all of us, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are being transformed into the same image." For with the sandal of the law loosed, he preached the gospel with the bare foot of free speech. The Jews held him and wanted to hinder him, but when the silver shone out in his sack, they tore their garments and turned back. For Paul's free preaching on behalf of Christ stripped the Jewish people bare and cut away all their grace,

and so they went back, who could not see what lay before them. Those who lose Christ go backward. So too in the gospel, when they seized the Lord Jesus to put him to death, they went backward and fell to the ground. Rightly did they turn back, who were falling away from that heavenly grace into earthly ruin. So in the moral sense they did not want to go back without their brother, and in the mystical sense they did not want to return without Paul, for they declared that if he were lost, the old age of their father, the people, would be brought down in grief.

And so Judah wished to remain with Joseph, so as not to see the evils that would befall his father; that is, he already foresaw the evils that were to come upon the Jewish people and wished to guard against them. But since this free preaching was not yet found in that figure of the leaders of the Jewish people, Joseph wept; that is, in him Jesus wept.

And he ordered everyone to withdraw, so that he might be made known to his brothers; for he had come, as he himself says, only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. And raising his voice with weeping, he said: "I am Joseph; is my father still alive?" That is: he stretched out his hands to a people unbelieving and contradicting, not seeking an envoy or a messenger, but himself the Lord, wishing to save his people. "I who spoke am here," he says, and "I have been made manifest to those who did not seek me, I appear to those who did not ask for me." What else, then, did he cry out at that time but "I am Jesus," when, tested by the leaders of the Jews who asked, "Are you the Son of God?", he answered, "You say that I am"; when he said to Pilate, "You say that I am a king; for this I was born"; when, to the high priest who said, "I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God," he replied, "You have said it. Truly I say to you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power and coming with the clouds of heaven"? This, then, is what he says: "I am Joseph, I am of divine power. Is my father still alive?" That is: "I do not deny my father, I acknowledge my brothers, if either you recognize your brother or the father his son. Is my people still alive, then, from whose family I have chosen a brother for myself?"

"Come near to me, for I have drawn near to you, and so far as to make myself a sharer in your nature by taking flesh. Do not flee even one who shares in your fellowship, if you do not recognize the author of salvation."

"And they came near to him," it says, "and he said: I am Joseph your brother, whom you handed over into Egypt. Now therefore do not be grieved, and let it not seem hard to you that you sold me here; for God sent me before you for life." What brotherly devotion, what sweet kinship, that he should even excuse a crime close to murdering his own kin, saying that it had come from divine providence, not from human wickedness, since he had not been offered up to death by men but sent to life by the Lord. What else does that intercession of our Lord Jesus Christ contain—who surpassed all brothers in devotion—when, placed on the cross, he said on behalf of the people: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing"? What else does that holy greeting contain, when he stood among his disciples and said: "Peace be with you; it is I, do not be afraid"? And when, troubled and terrified, they thought they were seeing a spirit, he said to them again: "Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." So these mysteries, which were to come in later times, were revealed even then.

Indeed, they are expressed in the very same words, so that we may understand that it is the same one who spoke first in Joseph and afterwards in his own body, since he did not even change the words. For he said then: "Do not be grieved," and further on: "Go up to my father and say to him: Thus says your son Joseph: God has made me lord of all the land of Egypt." And in the gospel he says: "Do not be afraid. Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me." And further on he says: "All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth," which is to say: "It was by divine ordering that I received power, not by human cruelty." He who recounts the reward does not cast up the crime.

And what he says in Genesis, "For God sent me before you for life," he repeats in the gospel, saying: "Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit"; for this is the reward and the life of the saints, that they have redeemed others as well.

Notice also that it was not written idly in Genesis: "And you shall be near me, you and your sons and your sons' sons"; for this is what he said in the gospel: "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age."

How plain, too, is that mystery: that, as though every command had been fulfilled, Joseph embraces his brother Benjamin and fell upon his neck, just as, when the gospel has been fulfilled, Christ embraces Paul with what we might call the arms of his mercy, so that he may lift him, bent down by his inward way of thinking, up to heaven, as if by the neck. Hence he too, raised up by Christ, says: "But our citizenship is in heaven."

And Pharaoh rejoiced that Joseph had recognized his brothers. So the news spread through Pharaoh's house, and he urged holy Joseph to invite his brothers to come with their father, and he orders their packs to be filled with wheat and wagons to be given them. Where would such kindness come from in a foreigner, unless that great mystery were being shown: that the Church no longer begrudges it when the Jews are redeemed, and the Christian people rejoice at this joining, and help with whatever support they can, and send those who preach the gospel of the kingdom of God, so that they may be called out sooner? To them two robes each are given.

And he singles out Paul, whose words he sets forth, on whom three hundred gold pieces and five robes of different colours are bestowed by Christ. He has three hundred gold pieces who preaches the cross of Christ, and so he says: "For I decided to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus and him crucified." And he rightly receives gold pieces, because he preached not in persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration of the Spirit. He receives five robes, either as the disciplines of manifold wisdom, or because he was not captured by any allurements of the bodily senses, but where others found danger he held victory; for he overcame all the pleasures of the flesh by singular self-control and virtue, and no bodily weakness dulled his mind or his zeal; while he was in the body, he was unaware that he had a body. Indeed, caught up into paradise, not knowing whether in the body or out of the body, he heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter. In short, he gave off no earthly scent while on earth, as he himself teaches, saying: "For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved."

Paul, then, excels, and his portion overflows; but the other preachers also have their own grace. They receive two robes each. Which ones? Surely those about which you ought to have no doubt, since you have read what was said of Wisdom: "She made double garments for her husband." One is mystical, the other moral. But not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all pastors, not all workers of miracles, not all have the gift of healing, not all speak in tongues. Where the rewards are different, the merits are different.

And gifts are sent ahead to the father too. The son honours his father; Christ invites his people with promises, invites them with gifts. Those asses carry these gifts—useless and toilsome before, now useful—carrying the gifts in a figure of Christ, as they were to carry the giver of gifts in the gospel.

Then he sent his brothers away and they departed. And Joseph said to them: "Do not quarrel on the way." How well he teaches that we must guard against anger, since it can separate even brothers who love one another, and that discord is especially to be shunned on a journey, where the very company of travellers ought to share an unbroken bond of goodwill. And what else did our Lord Jesus say, when he was about to depart from this body and was sending his disciples away, but that they should not quarrel on the way, when he said: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you"? For where there is peace, anger has no place, discord is banished, dissension is put to flight. This, then, is what he says: "My peace I give to you," that is, "Do not quarrel on the way." And consider whether by "on this way" he means that indignation is to be avoided along this whole course of life, since anger often leads even the innocent into wrongdoing; for while we grow angry more than is just and want to restrain another's sin, we commit graver sins. So the apostle says: "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath," that is, let us turn aside from it, so that it does not seize us. Hence also the Lord Jesus, sending his disciples out to preach the gospel, sent them without gold, without silver, without money, without a staff—that is, so as to take away both the incitements to strife and the instruments of revenge.

"And they went up," it says, "out of Egypt and came into the land of Canaan to Jacob their father, and told him, saying: Joseph your son is alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." What is the land of Canaan? The land that was wavering. What, then, could more plainly signify the times of the apostles, when they entered the synagogues of the wavering Jews and preached the power of the Lord Jesus, as we have in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter says: "This Jesus [?] God raised up, of which we are witnesses. Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this gift which you see"? We notice, surely, how he says both that he is alive and that he is ruler of the whole earth, he who opens his storehouses of spiritual grace and gives abundance to all. The apostles said these things, but the Jews did not believe; instead they laid hands on them and thrust the preachers of salvation into prison.

Hence it is also written of Jacob: "He was dismayed in mind, for he did not believe them." He was dismayed with the feeling of an unbelieving people; but after he learned of Christ's deeds, soothed by such great benefits and works, he took heart again, saying: "It is a great thing for me if my son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die." The first and greatest foundation of faith is to believe in the resurrection of Christ. For whoever has believed that he was raised seeks him in haste, approaches him devoutly, and worships God in his inmost mind; for he believes that he himself will not die, if he believes in the author of the resurrection.
And Israel arose and came to the well of the oath, and offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac.

Whoever hastens to Christ is rightly raised up. Faith comes before devotion. First he raised himself up, and afterwards he offered sacrifice; for that person sacrifices well who has searched out the knowledge of the Godhead.

And God spoke to Israel in a vision by night, saying: “Jacob, Jacob.” He said: “What is it?” And God said: “I am the God of your fathers. Do not be afraid; go down into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will bring you out for ever.” How it is that they do not understand what they themselves read, and deny Moses whom they praise, since they refuse to believe his writings! What could be clearer than that in this passage they are being invited to cross over to the Church of God, so that those who were formerly hemmed in within the narrow borders of Judea might move over to the people of God, which, gathered together from the whole world, from all nations and peoples, has become a great nation? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth. So Jacob is called by his sons; that is, the Jewish people is invited to grace by Peter, John and Paul.

Our God himself also encourages him with his own oracle and promises him progress in faith, the fruit of his gift, saying to him: “Joseph will put his hand upon your eyes.” The holy patriarch was surely not anxious about who would close his eyes, although even on a simple understanding a moral feeling is expressed here. For if we often long to embrace those we love, how much more, when we are about to depart from this body, do we delight in that last touch of our dear children and find comfort in it as provision for the journey! Yet we may understand it mystically to mean that the Jewish people would come to know God later. For this is the mystery: that the true Joseph will put his hands upon its eyes, so that the one who did not see before may now see. Come to the Gospel; read how that blind man was healed, on whom Jesus laid his hand and took away his blindness. For Christ does not lay his hand on those who are going to die, but on those who are going to live; or if on those who are going to die, then rightly so, because we die first in order to come back to life. For we cannot live to God unless we first die to sin.

So seventy-five souls went down into Egypt, as it is written, and this, mystically, is the number of remission, because after such great hardness of heart and such great sins they would be held unworthy unless the remission of sins were granted to them. Judah meets him, that is, the confession of error. The Jewish people, as it is about to come, sends him ahead as its herald. That is why the true Joseph also comes to meet them, that is, the judge and interpreter of the Godhead, because confession now goes ahead of those whom faithlessness formerly held in its possession. For Christ is the interpreter of the Godhead, since no one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known. In the last times he will receive the Jewish people, now old in years and weary, not according to its merits but according to the election of his grace, and he will lay his hand upon its eyes to take away its blindness. He put off its healing so that the one who before had not thought it right to believe might believe last, and might lose the prerogative of its earlier election. Hence the Apostle also says: “A blindness has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel would be saved.”

The deeds of the patriarchs, then, are mysteries of things to come. Indeed, Jacob himself says to his sons: “Gather together, so that I may tell you what will befall you in the last days. Gather together and listen to Israel your father.”
